content: The findings from various studies highlight the effectiveness of different interventions aimed at improving HIV prevention, education, and care in prison settings. Below is a detailed summary of the key findings and recommendations: 1. Safer Sex Practices and HIV Education: Studies in the USA (Derlega et al., 2008) identified stigma and misinformation about HIV transmission among inmates. Peer-based HIV education programs were recommended to reduce stigma and improve knowledge. A brief Transtheoretical Model (TTM)-based HIV education program in Taiwan (Ko et al., 2009) was effective for drug-dependent inmates. This program included a one-hour lecture on HIV transmission, prevention, and treatment, as well as skill-building sessions on safe injection practices, needle cleaning, and condom use. 2. Behavioral Interventions: In the USA, a DVD-based intervention (Martin et al., 2008) reduced unprotected sexual intercourse compared to standard interventions. Feedback emphasized the need for brief and simple interventions. Project START (Grinstead et al., 2008) demonstrated that enhanced interventions (multiple sessions) were more effective than single-session interventions in reducing sexual risk behaviors. Incentives were provided at weeks one and twelve. In Switzerland, structured information exchange (StIE) models were used to educate prisoners about HIV and Hepatitis C at the start of their sentences (Fluhmann et al., 2012). 3. HIV Testing and Counseling: Mandatory testing was deemed unethical and counterproductive. Rapid HIV testing was found to significantly improve the odds of receiving test results compared to conventional testing (Beckwith et al., 2010). In Washington State jails, switching to opt-out testing increased testing rates from 5% to 90% (Strick et al., 2011). In Jamaica, a demonstration project offering mandatory opt-out testing for new prisoners and voluntary testing for long-term inmates achieved high acceptance rates (Andrinopoulos et al., 2010). 4. HIV Care and Treatment: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has significantly reduced mortality rates among incarcerated individuals in countries where ART is accessible. However, challenges such as stigma, lack of privacy, and poor relationships with prison health staff negatively impacted adherence (Robertson et al., 2009; Shalihu et al., 2014). Continuity of care between prison and community settings is critical. Discharge planning and linkage to community care were emphasized to prevent health gains made during incarceration from being lost (Fontana et al., 2007; Wohl et al., 2011). 5. Needle and Syringe Exchange Programs (NSPs): Evidence supports the feasibility and effectiveness of NSPs in reducing needle-sharing and HIV transmission in prisons. Additional benefits include reduced overdose risk and improved access to drug dependence treatment (Moller et al., 2008; Milloy et al., 2013). In Kyrgyzstan, needle-sharing decreased from 20% to 8% after implementing NSPs in two prisons (Moller et al., 2008). 6. Sexual Violence in Prisons: Sexual violence in prisons poses significant health risks, including HIV transmission. Structural interventions like cameras and housing inmates by risk level were also effective (Yap et al., 2007; La Vigne et al., 2011). 7. Condom Distribution: Studies in the USA and Australia demonstrated that condom distribution in prisons does not increase sexual activity but promotes safer sex practices. This intervention is cost-effective and reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections (Butler et al., 2013; Leibowitz et al., 2012). 8. HIV Prevention for Vulnerable Groups: Programs targeting specific populations, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender individuals, included condom distribution, HIV education, and STI counseling. These interventions were effective in reducing HIV and STI prevalence (Harawa et al., 2010; Tuli et al., 2009). 9. Barriers to HIV Care: Barriers such as stigma, discrimination, lack of trust in healthcare professionals, and insufficient nutritional support were identified as challenges to ART adherence and HIV prevention efforts. Addressing these barriers through education and stigma reduction strategies is essential (Motshabi et al., 2011; Shalihu et al., 2014). 10. Recommendations: Prison systems should implement comprehensive HIV prevention programs, including education, condom distribution, NSPs, and access to ART. Voluntary, confidential HIV testing and counseling should be made easily accessible to all prisoners. Efforts should focus on ensuring continuity of care between prison and community settings, particularly for ART and opioid substitution therapy (OST). Structural interventions, such as cameras and staff training, should be adopted to prevent sexual violence and improve safety in prisons. These findings underscore the importance of tailored, evidence-based interventions to address the unique challenges of HIV prevention, care, and treatment in prison settings.
